---
title: "Glossary"
---

Terms are listed alphabetically. This glossary grows with milestone M1
(definition) in the [roadmap](../ROADMAP.md).

**Causal structure**
: A representation (typically a directed acyclic graph, or DAG) of the
assumed cause-and-effect relationships among variables, used to reason
about what interventions would change health outcomes [@pearl2009].

**Construct**
: The thing a measurement is intended to represent — for example the state
of health, or one of its domains. Constructs are real but not directly
observable; measurements of them are
[proxies](#proxy). See the [definition of the state of
health](../explanation/definition-of-health.qmd).

**Data**
: Construed broadly: any publicly available information that can be
appropriately used for the project's goals — from microdata through
published summary statistics, indicator tables, dashboards, and report
figures.

**Definition (provisional)**
: The project's working definition of the state of health. It is
versioned and expected to evolve as the project learns what is
measurable; each revision records its trigger and its changes. See the
[definition document](../explanation/definition-of-health.qmd).

**Diátaxis**
: The documentation framework this site follows, organising docs into
four modes: tutorials, how-to guides, reference, and explanation
[@procidadiataxis].

**Health authority**
: One of the regional organisations delivering health services in BC
(e.g. Vancouver Coastal Health, Fraser Health) [@bcHealthAuthorities]. A
common geographic breakdown for BC health data.

**Indicator**
: A defined, sourced, reproducible measurement used to represent some
aspect of the state of health (e.g. life expectancy at birth). An
indicator is a [proxy](#proxy), never the construct itself.

**Measurement framework**
: The scheme of domains and candidate indicators that operationalises the
project's definition of the state of health. See the [measurement
framework](../reference/measurement-framework.qmd).

**Multilevel model**
: A statistical model in which data at more than one level of resolution
(e.g. individuals within regions) are modelled jointly, allowing
information to be shared across levels [@gelman2007]. One of the ways the
project fuses pictures at different resolutions.

**Nonstationarity**
: The property of a series or relationship whose statistical properties
(level, variability, association with other variables) change over time
[@box2015; @hyndman2021]. The project assumes BC's health is
nonstationary in all three senses; see [Health is not
stationary](../explanation/nonstationarity.qmd).

**Observation window**
: The time period a reported result was estimated on. Every published
figure in this project carries its observation window, because a result
true for one window may not hold for another.

**Proxy**
: A measurement used in place of a construct that cannot be observed
directly — every indicator in this project is a proxy. Proxies carry
measurement error and construct error, and can drift over time; they are
never identical with the state of health they track. See [Proxies are not
the state of health](../explanation/definition-of-health.qmd#proxies-are-not-the-state-of-health).

**Regime shift**
: An abrupt change in the level or behaviour of a series — e.g. an
epidemic, health system reform, or coding definition change — after
which the series is effectively a different one. Comparisons spanning a
regime shift are treated separately from comparisons within a regime.

**Resolution**
: The level at which a datum or result is observed — individual,
neighbourhood, HSDA, health authority, provincial, or external/non-BC.
This project uses all available resolutions and records the resolution of
every result.

**State of health (SoH)**
: The condition of health in a population at a point in time and space —
the central quantity this project describes and predicts. Defined
provisionally in the [definition
document](../explanation/definition-of-health.qmd).

**Stationarity**
: The opposite of nonstationarity: a series or relationship whose
statistical properties hold steady over the analysis window. Pooled
single estimates are only reported when stationarity is supported
[@box2015; @hyndman2021]; see [Health is not
stationary](../explanation/nonstationarity.qmd).
